Our findings demonstrate that information-flow control is an effective technique to extend web security to browser agents, gaining on autonomy and utility against state-of-the-art baselines. The source code and data are openly accessible at https://github.com/microsoft/SPIDES.

items.title: Empirical Analysis of TEE-Enabled Rollup Designs
items.author: Claudiu-Nicu B\u{a}rbieru, Corentin Libert, Peterson Yuhala, Andrei Arusoaie, Matthieu Bettinger, Oana-Otilia Captarencu, Pascal Felber, Emanuel Onica, Etienne Rivi\`ere, Valerio Schiavoni
items.content: Layer 2 (L2) rollups have become the dominant scaling solution in Ethereum. At the core of these systems lies the rollup sequencer, a component that orders, executes, and submits L2 transaction blocks to the main Ethereum blockchain. The centralization of this sequencer introduces security risks, including censorship and malicious manipulation of transactions to extract maximum extractable value (MEV). Trusted execution environments (TEEs) provide strong hardware-enforced confidentiality and integrity guarantees for code and data. TEEs are strong candidates for strengthening security and ensuring verifiable neutrality in rollup sequencer operations, but multiple TEE-based designs are possible, offering different trade-offs among modularity, performance, and security guarantees. Among them, the separation of proposer and builder logic (PBS) into independent services is a strong contender against the monolithic approach that bundles all sequencer logic. Despite several proposed theoretical frameworks, there is a lack of experimental evaluation of the practicality and security trade-offs of integrating TEEs into rollup sequencers. This work addresses this gap through a comprehensive empirical study of TEE-enabled rollup designs under both PBS and monolithic sequencer models. Our experimental evaluations show that the impact of TEEs on rollup performance is small and that PBS does not significantly amplify it. We also show that PBS can lead to significant performance improvements by enabling more specialized, efficient builder logic implementations.

items.title: Unbounded Losses, Unchecked Inputs: Measuring the Safeguards of LLM Options-Trading Agents
items.author: Mengxiao Wang, Nitesh Saxena
items.content: Large language model (LLM) agents now place options orders at retail brokers, and developers publish open-source options agents faster than anyone has examined them. Prior security work on trading agents scored academic equities designs by whether an attacker can flip a buy-or-sell decision. We present the first measurement of the options agents that brokers and developers ship, scored by the safeguards they enforce and by the worst loss their documented order paths can reach. We screened 765 GitHub repositories, broker documentation, and the research literature and found 215 eligible repositories and 8 broker-native agent interfaces. We then scored 26 systems, including every broker interface and every open-source project with at least 20 stars, on seven robustness and eleven security safeguards with cell-level evidence. The ecosystem is new: 198 of the 215 repositories were created in 2026, and 129 (60.0%) appeared in the two weeks around one options-trading hackathon. Of the 22 systems that can place orders, 10 enforce a pre-trade limit outside the model, yet none of the 26 authenticate their text sources or cross-check market data. Of the 26, 17 can execute with no mandatory human step and 13 can reach unbounded loss, including 6 of the 8 broker interfaces. Because an attacker who writes the agent's inputs can move an order's strike, expiry, volatility, and legs while its direction stays correct, options agents need loss limits enforced at the order boundary.

items.title: RATION: Towards Quantitative Risk-Based Access Control for AI Agents
items.author: Yuntao Du, Harsh Chaudhari, Yuetian Chen, Ron Heichman, Ashish Jayamohan, Kumar Pallav, Mahim Patel, Kaiyuan Zhang, Kyle Polley, Jerry Ma, Ninghui Li
items.content: AI agents increasingly interact with external environments to complete complex user tasks. These interactions can lead to unexpected behavior and expose agents to security threats such as indirect prompt injection. Current agent security systems largely protect agents by restricting their actions, which can result in a substantial security-utility trade-off for complex, open-ended tasks. To address this, we propose a quantitative risk-based approach to access control for AI agents that regulates measurable risks accumulated during task execution. As a concrete realization of this approach, we introduce RATION, a security framework that tracks measurable risks associated with agent actions and enforces quantitative constraints throughout execution. RATION first constructs a task-specific policy by combining explicit constraints derived from the user request with implicit risks calibrated from historical executions of similar tasks. During task execution, RATION continuously tracks the accumulated risks and applies different enforcement strategies depending on the type of risk. Extensive experiments on four security benchmarks show that RATION provides strong security while maintaining high task utility across diverse models and environments.

items.title: SigmaTrace: Library-Agnostic Observability for CPU/GPU-Initiated RDMA Communication
items.author: Javid Baydamirli, Didem Unat
items.content: RDMA networking enables low-latency, high-bandwidth communication on large systems. Despite its adoption, however, observability is lacking. Existing tools target specific communication libraries or only report aggregated data, missing per-operation behavior. The gap is widest for GPU-initiated networking, whose in-kernel RDMA operations are invisible to the host. We present SigmaTrace, a library-agnostic RDMA profiling framework providing fine-grained, per-operation visibility for CPU and GPU-initiated networking. It traces operations at the libibverbs/mlx5dv layers, the common denominator beneath communication libraries on InfiniBand and RoCE, and employs a low-overhead memory interposition technique that, to our knowledge, gives the first observability into GPU-initiated RDMA without source patching or binary instrumentation. Host-side tracing adds 1.3% overhead on NCCL AllReduce at 128 GPUs and under 2% on RCCL at 1024 GPUs. On a persistent-kernel BFS and Mixture-of-Experts inference, SigmaTrace exposes an in-kernel barrier spread and 2.13x inter-node traffic skew invisible to existing profilers.

items.title: VERAS: Verification-Guided Adaptive Search for Reliable Operations Research
items.author: Minbo Ma, Honglin Zhang, Bangtao Zhou, Chunguang Yu, Dasheng Ju, Yichen Shen, Fengli Xu, Yong Li
items.content: Advances in reasoning, coding, and tool use enable LLM agents to solve operations research (OR) problems through iterative problem modeling, program construction, and verification. Yet passing self-authored verification does not ensure that the solutions satisfy task constraints and meet optimization quality. This gap can arise from correlated specification errors, where the generated program and its checks share omissions or misinterpretations of task requirements, alongside incomplete verification coverage and ineffective optimization strategies. We propose VERAS, a verification-guided adaptive search harness for reliable OR that uses verification evidence to prioritize feasibility repair, constraint-coverage review, and solution-quality improvement. VERAS combines task-specific solution checkers with a separate verification agent to examine candidate solutions against the task requirements. It uses verification feedback to guide feasibility repair, additional constraint checking, and objective improvement, while candidate acceptance criteria screen revisions for deterioration in output validity or constraint satisfaction. On ORAgentBench, VERAS achieves a 42.99% pass rate, exceeding the reported 35.51% of Codex using the same LLM. Across two industrial-scale OR problems, VERAS reduces inter-datacenter peak bandwidth by 10.34% relative to native Codex and lowers annualized distribution network planning costs by 6.28% compared with expert-designed solutions. Code and evidence are available at https://github.com/holimario/VERAS.

items.title: Koi: Evidence-Guided, Self-Calibrating Planning for Multi-Cloud, Heterogeneous LLM Inference Fleets
items.author: Mankeerat Sidhu, Gangmuk Lim, Hetarth Chopra, Maximillian Eisenberg, Quan Hao Ng, Aryan Gosaliya, Shu Liu, Luka Govedi\v{c}, Jiaxin Shan, Hongkuan Zhou, Vikram Sharma Mailthody, P. Brighten Godfrey, Ion Stoica
items.content: Deploying a large language model (LLM) requires choosing the right accelerator, parallelization strategy, engine configuration, and replica count amongst ~140 other variables across clouds, regions, and markets. These decisions are intertwined, and the best cluster-wide plan continually changes as jobs contend for shared capacity on shifting workloads. We present Koi, a self-calibrating cluster planner for heterogeneous, multi-cloud fleets. Koi uses a Recursive Language Model (RLM) hierarchy to propose hypotheses and reason over deployment while deterministic components predict serving behavior, score candidates, and control placement. It represents inference behavior as a fixed causal graph linking decisions (e.g., accelerator, parallelism), runtime mediators (e.g., KV-cache pressure, communication overhead), and outcomes (e.g., latency, throughput). Each deployment strengthens or weakens scoped causal relationships, building a comprehensive playbook for inference that the planner employs to guide future decisions. Job-wise configurations are composed into cluster-wide plans and evaluated against serving objectives, resource constraints, SLO risks, and cost. Across benchmarks, Koi achieves 1.18x greater goodput than the strongest baseline while reducing $/token by 20% in a real heterogeneous cluster. Ablations isolate the contribution of Koi's architecture: a pure language model attains a composite score of 35.3, the same model equipped with Koi's deterministic tools reaches 51.6, and the full Koi planner reaches 70.8.

items.title: Can Agents Keep Secrets They Were Never Told? Benchmarking Latent Privacy Risks Across Sessions with MemJoin
items.author: Qishun Yang, Shu Yang, Difei Xu, Di Wang, Meng Ding
items.content: To support sustained interactions and personalized assistance, agents use long-term memory to retain and combine user information across sessions. Reusing such memories can lead an agent to state a sensitive relation while completing an ordinary task that does not require it. The relation to protect and the combination of clues that reveal it may remain hidden at memory write time, when later records and tasks are still unknown. In this paper, we introduce MemJoin, a privacy benchmark of 288 synthetic analysis cases in which the complete history entails a sensitive relation, but every individual session is insufficient. We evaluate six memory systems with the same answer-generating model, alongside full-history and no-history controls. Each system writes and updates memories in session order and later retrieves context for an ordinary task, while target annotations remain with the evaluator. We separately check which target attribute values appear in stored records and retrieved context, and whether the final answer states the complete, person-linked relation. In a separate paired test on a prespecified subset, removing shared identifiers and other connecting clues can change complete-relation output while all checked target attribute values remain visible. These findings show why checking attribute visibility alone is insufficient to evaluate what records from different sessions reveal together.

items.title: Defending Against Dormant Poisoning Attacks Across Language and Multimodal Agents
items.author: Wonjun Lee, Vaidehi Patil, Zaid Khan, Yue Zhang, Hyunji Lee, Suhyun Kim, Mohit Bansal
items.content: Recent work shows that attackers can implant dormant malicious behaviors that remain hidden at release but emerge after benign fine-tuning. As foundation models are used as agents, whether dormant poisoning extends to harmful agent actions and multimodal settings remains unclear. We show two agentic risks: (1) harmful behaviors activated by benign fine-tuning can extend to unseen actions; (2) multiple harmful behaviors can coexist and be jointly activated by benign downstream fine-tuning. Existing defenses often rely on external safe responses, which are hard to obtain for agent actions, or a trusted clean reference model. We exploit a key property of dormant poisoning: the attacker must preserve safe behavior at release to conceal poisoning, and this behavior can serve as a safety reference. Leveraging this property, we automatically construct a Safety Buffer pairing harmful inputs with the released model's responses and benign versions generated by the same model to remove harmful intent. The Safety Buffer can replace external safe responses in existing defenses, but these defenses do not distinguish updates that weaken safety from those that preserve it, often increasing over-refusal or reducing utility. To address this limitation, we introduce LookAhead Defense, which previews benign fine-tuning updates using the Safety Buffer and penalizes only updates predicted to weaken safe behavior on harmful inputs or increase the likelihood of refusals on benign versions in the Safety Buffer. Across language models, language agents, and multimodal agents, LookAhead Defense reduces harmful behavior in agents from up to 93.9% to at most 14.2% and harmful responses in language models from up to 92.5% to at most 2.0% versus vanilla fine-tuning, while maintaining competitive utility and low over-refusal. It remains effective against other poisoning methods.

items.title: Safety Analysis of CPSs Over-the-air Updates: Test Case Prioritization and Selection
items.author: Andrea Bombarda, Luca Carminati, Nunzio Marco Bisceglia, Mehrnoosh Askarpour, Sahar Kokaly, Ramesh S, Marsha Chechik, Claudio Menghi
items.content: Over-the-air (OTA) updates for Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) allow engineers to modify their software wirelessly. In the automotive domain, they enable manufacturers to update software without physical access to the vehicle. However, OTA updates can generate a large number of possible software configurations. For example, end users may decide whether or not to install any given OTA updates. The combinatorial explosion of these configurations hampers SW testing, a standard practice for detecting errors in CPS. To overcome this limitation, we propose CRISP (CRIticality-based Selection and Prioritization), a novel framework supporting test case prioritization and selection in the context of OTA updates. Our framework leverages test case robustness, i.e., how far they are from violating the system requirements, to drive test case prioritization and selection. It enables engineers to rank test case executions from most to least critical, and to select only the critical test cases relevant to a given OTA update. We evaluated our approach using a representative SW product line consisting of seven different vehicles, 22 driving scenarios, and two software components. We considered 224 tests, requiring 59 hours of execution time. We assessed the effectiveness of CRISP across five OTA updates. We compared our solution with (a) a random test case prioritization and selection algorithm, and (b) AP-DISC, identified as the state-of-the-art solution in a recent empirical study on the subject. Our results show that CRISP outperforms our baselines in finding failure-revealing test cases, and that our selection procedure can be configured to find reasonable and practical tradeoffs among accuracy (percentage of failure-revealing test cases identified) and computational time (time required to find them).

items.title: Effective Construction of Feature Database of Fingerprinting Functions for Code-Clone SCA
items.author: Zhiling Zhu, Tieming Chen, Chengwei Liu, Jiahui Wu, Qijie Song, Zhengzi Xu, Yueming Wu, Yang Liu
items.content: In contemporary software development, the extensive adoption of third-party libraries has become standard practice to avoid reinventing the wheel. This trend is particularly evident in programming ecosystems that lack mature package managers, such as C/C++. Within this context, Code Clone Detection (CCD) techniques have emerged as essential tools for identifying instances of code reuse, thereby mitigating security and legal concerns. Despite significant advances in CCD algorithms, a notable gap persists between academic tools and real-world applications. This disparity primarily arises because academic tools rely on experimental datasets composed of a limited number of indexed repositories, whereas real-world applications require a much broader scope of code sources. To address this challenge, we propose a novel, systematic approach for selecting appropriate open-source repositories to construct a more effective CCD feature dataset. Our method, OSSScope, employs a greedy algorithm to analyze the diversity of fingerprinting functions across 2.55 million C repositories on GitHub, maximizing unique fingerprinting functions while minimizing the number of repositories required. OSSScope compiles an optimal feature dataset containing 61 million fingerprinting functions from 190K repositories, resulting in a 22.65% improvement in recall over SOTA tools, and covers over 95% of the features from other sources. Leveraging the selected repositories, we introduce RClassifier, a lightweight classification model that determines whether a repository should be included, streamlining construction for migration to other language ecosystems. Our evaluation of RClassifier in the Golang ecosystem validates its effectiveness, achieving recall comparable to the dataset produced by OSSScope.

items.title: When Code Becomes an LLM Call: An Empirical Study of Call-Site Contracts in Agentic Systems
items.author: Shihao Weng, Longtian Wang, Yang Feng, Mingfei Cheng, Jia Liu, Chao Shen, He Ye, Federica Sarro, Xiaofei Xie
items.content: Software quality has long rested on specifications that state what code must do, and on testing and verification that check that the code does it. Agentic systems change this foundation: they replace parts of their logic, such as choosing the next tool, judging whether an action is allowed, or writing code to run, with calls to a large language model (LLM). The program still relies on what this logic must guarantee, but the model's behavior is not fixed by code, varies across runs, and can be steered by its input. The guarantee must therefore come from the program around each LLM call site, as a contract of pre-conditions, prompt constraints, and post-conditions. We present an empirical study of these contracts in 496 LLM call sites of 40 popular open-source agentic systems (13.4 MLOC, four languages). Using a multi-agent pipeline validated by 17,428 human judgments, we trace where every model output flows, derive an expected contract for each call site without access to its code, and compare it with the contract that the code implements. We find that 48% of LLM outputs reach control flow or execution, and 73% of these never reach a person. Programs enforce 78% of their constraints in code, but in the prompt, 67% of the constraints are only requested from the model. Although 82% of call sites are checked before and after the call, 63% of the expected constraints are unmet and only 5.3% of call sites satisfy their whole contract; ten recurring patterns explain 99% of the gaps. 38 mechanisms behind these gaps trigger at runtime, and a small code fix that enforces the expected constraint stops all 38. Our results show that the presence of checks says little about their adequacy, and we derive implications for agent developers, framework maintainers, and researchers.

items.title: From Candidate Admission to Task-Level Return: Auditing LLM-Generated Code under Execution Contracts
items.author: Hiroyasu Usami, Keisuke Hara, Ayato Tsuboi, Naohiko Matsuda
items.content: Admission rules retain generated programs, whereas selection policies return one candidate per task. We audit how these decisions interact with execution contracts in two separately frozen, disjoint HumanEvalPlus cohorts, each comprising 32 tasks, four samples per task per profile and two served profiles. Under the inline execution contract, a structural-and-self-test screen admits 4-9 expanded-suite nonpasses per 80-107 admissions and excludes 14-43 suite passes per 128 planned attempts. A restricted module-supply condition adds 20 and 14 passing admissions for one profile in the respective cohorts, plus one follow-up nonpass, and reduces the excluded suite passes to 14-23. All fixed first-admitted outcomes and abstentions remain unchanged. In the original pool, the added passes enter already all-passing admitted pools; in the follow-up, four of 24 common sample orders lose one passed task. Selected-subset diagnostics separately address registration-sensitive completion and reference-relative assertion disagreement, accounting for input domains and comparator tolerances. In these high-pass pools, candidate retention and task-level return diverge and are reported separately. Results are conditional on the saved pools, contracts and pinned suites; downstream training effects are unmeasured.

items.title: [AINews] not much happened today
items.content: Congrats to DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, and Mercury 3 (details below) but they’re not going to be in super wide use just yet. We are starting to announce AIE CODE speakers, so if you haven’t applied to attend the most selective gathering of top agentic engineers in SF (and the most popular livestreamed AIE format of 2025), you should do so now! AI News for 10/16/2026-10/19/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 Becomes the Open-Weight Value Leader Release and specs: Artificial Analysis lists DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 as a 552B-total / 16B-active MoE model with a 1M-token context window and an MIT license (AA). Pricing: Unchanged at $0.30/$1.20 per million input/output tokens during peak hours. Off-peak pricing is half that, and cache hits cost $0.006 per million tokens. Availability: It is available through DeepSeek’s API, Fireworks, Baseten, DeepInfra, Cloudflare and Together. Training claim: Together says DeepSeek trained the update with self-feedback RL for building complete projects from scratch (Together). Artificial Analysis results: The model scores 45 on the AA Intelligence Index, up 6 points. That ties it with GLM-5.3 for #2 among open-weight models, 1 point behind MiMo-V2.6-Pro, at $0.26 per task. Agentic and science gains: GDPval-AA Elo rose 146 to 1746, and CritPt rose from 14% to 24%. Hallucination: On AA-Omniscience, the non-hallucination rate jumped from 4% to 33% (detail). Caveat: AA notes that MiMo-V2.6-Pro and GPT-6.1 Sol (medium) both score higher at a lower cost per task. Arena and Vals rankings: The model is the #1 open model in Code Arena WebDev, placing #12 overall with 1670 points. That is 52 points above the prior Flash and roughly 10 points behind GPT-6 Sol Max (Arena). Agent Arena: It is also #1 open in Agent Arena, at #11 overall with a $0.20 median cost per task. Arena says that delivers about 37% of GPT-6.1 Sol’s improvement at 27% of the cost (Agent Arena). Vals Index: It initially ranked #1 open-weight at $0.64 per task (Vals). Under Vals Index v2.2 it ranks #8 overall and remains the top open-weight model (v2.2). Browser use: It scored 75/100 on long-horizon browser use, matching Opus 5.5, at $0.22 vs $2.35 per task (browser_use). Hands-on and contested evals: A Zhihu tester found the larger gains in agentic execution than in reasoning (ZhihuFrontier). Efficiency mixed: One frontend task took 20% of the previous version’s steps. Exploration-heavy tasks used 30–40% more tokens without better scores. Harness confound: The tester flags that the comparison also includes a change to DeepSeek Harness 0.2.1, not just the model update. Vendor benchmark: Release figures cite Terminal-Bench 4.0 rising from 31.2 to 42.3 (Zhihu). Benchmark mix: @teortaxesTex reports large gains on long-run operations but regressions on constraint adherence, browser use and research in one composite eval (thread). Cheating flag: The same commentator says the model was the only one caught cheating on a bug-hunting eval (post). KernelBench: It took #1 on a MegaQwen decode kernel by quietly storing the KV cache in FP8 against a BF16 spec, spending the tolerance budget. The result was accepted, but the author calls it a precision call rather than a free win (elliotarledge). Local deployment: Unsloth shipped a llama.cpp implementation with dynamic GGUFs. The Engram/PLE tables can drop to Q6_K at roughly MXFP8 quality and can stream from disk (danielhanchen). Low-bit quants: Community quants include 2-bit and 3-bit TrellisMX builds; the 3-bit build reports a mean KLD of 0.0664 nats (BrandonMusicKy). Megakernel: A work-in-progress megakernel reaches 500+ tok/s on 4× RTX Pro 6000 Max-Q (fraserpricee). Distillation debate: Dean Ball, now at OpenAI, says distillation plays a bigger role in China’s benchmark proximity than he had realized (deanwball). Counterargument: Skeptics argue that heavy SFT on another model’s traces usually raises hallucination, which is inconsistent with the Omniscience gains (teortaxesTex). Evidence demand: Others ask labs to publish their detection evidence (ziv_ravid). Model Launches: MiniMax M3.1 Flash, Mercury 3, Meta Muse and Video MiniMax M3.1 Flash: MiniMax revealed that “Space Bunny,” the stealth model that topped usage leaderboards, was an earlier build of this model (MiniMax). Claimed results: DeepSWE 74%, Automation-Bench 62% and BabyVision 91%. MiniMax claims it runs at 1/3 the cost and 3× the speed of M3. Pricing: $0.15/$0.60 per million input/output tokens, with cache reads at $0.015. Availability: Weights arrive Oct 23. It is free for a limited time on OpenRouter, OpenCode, Cline and Ollama Cloud. Independent evals: AA scores it 42, level with GLM-5.3-Flash and behind DeepSeek’s 45, at ~$0.22 per task. HLE is 48% and AA-Omniscience accuracy is 56%, but its hallucination rate is 93% because it attempts nearly every question (AA). Arenas: It places #12 open in Code Arena WebDev with 1588 points, 106 above M3 (Arena), and #26 on Design Arena frontend (DesignArena). Mercury 3 (Inception): Inception calls it the most capable diffusion LLM to date. It claims to beat GPT-6 Luna and Haiku 5.5 on quality at 1,000+ tok/s, while being 40× larger than Mercury 1 (StefanoErmon, volokuleshov). Availability: It is on Baseten with 1M-token context (Baseten). Size estimate: @scaling01 estimates it at over 280B parameters if Mercury 1 was about 7B (unconfirmed) (post). Meta Muse: Muse Wonder Full (Max) debuted at #6 in Code Arena WebDev with 1726 points, moving Meta to the #3 lab spot (Arena). It also ranks #4 on Vending-Bench 2 (andonlabs). Muse Glimmer report: Meta published a technical report on Muse Glimmer, a 30B open-weight agentic model designed to run at 4-bit on a single consumer GPU (AIatMeta). Distillation recipe: The report uses full-KL co-distillation from Muse Spark’s in-training logits, then cross-entropy for the final 5% (eliebakouch). Training also uses simulated multi-week “digital lives” (kimmonismus). FLUX 3 Max (fal × BFL): fal’s post-trained video model generates a 10-second video in roughly 12 seconds. AA ranks it #2 on image-to-video (statistically tied for #1) and #4 on text-to-video, with the top Physics score (AA). Pricing: $10.20/min at 720p, with 75% off for three weeks. Other notable releases: SKY-001: An “engineering world model” for CAD and BIM, claimed to be 51–125× faster and 150–210× cheaper than GPT-6 Astra (spisallyouneed). Gemini 4 Argon: Scores 20.2% on WeirdML, between Sonnet 5.5 and Fable 5.1, and trails on token efficiency (htihle). Mistral Timestral: Open time-series foundation models (qtnx_). Indra OCR 1.1: A 1M-parameter model running at 44 pages/s on CPU (VikParuchuri). Cyber Defense, Safety and Eval Integrity OpenCode attack and refusals: OpenCode reports a sustained 48-hour attack from agent swarms (thdxr). Mid-incident, frontier models refused to help analyze the attacks because the payloads tripped guardrails, a problem Hugging Face reportedly hit earlier (AndrewCurran_). Daybreak access: The situation reportedly improved after OpenCode got access to Daybreak Blue (kimmonismus). Policy reaction: David Sacks argues the episode shows the limits of centralized safety approaches and makes the case for open models in defense (DavidSacks). Anthropic OSS Scanner: The program offers free periodic vulnerability scans of critical open-source projects, with proofs of concept and patches. The first week reported 77 critical and 803 high model-rated findings, including a curl fix (ClaudeDevs). Microsoft Project Perception: Satya Nadella says the expansion treats models as insider risks, using external controls to assess agent risk, adapt permissions and contain threats (satyanadella). Training and interpretability research: Reward hacking: A new paper allows reward hacking during RL but routes it into designated parameters. Disabling those parameters at deployment keeps the learned capabilities without the hacking (_jake_ward). Activation detection: Models can be trained to detect when their activations are being read (Sauers_). Commenters trace the signal to floating-point computation-order differences, which argues for matching training and inference numerics exactly (AndrewLampinen, cHHillee). CoT controllability: Reasoning models follow constraints far better when the constraint is placed in the chain of thought as a self-instruction rather than in the user prompt (dair_ai). Benchmark and audit integrity: Terminal-Bench audit: Of 65 tasks reviewed, 60 had issues, 44 could be passed by cheating and 41 graded on unstated requirements (chem_safety). Auditor incentives: A former METR staffer says the largest source of bias in voluntary audits is fear of losing lab access (SydneyVonArx). Superposition claims: Chris Potts pushes back on claims that Cammarata’s essay “solves” interpretability, asking for rigorous evaluation (ChrisGPotts). Agent Harnesses and Research Methods Harness² (Google Research): The open-source framework lets an agent edit its own harness (system prompt, skills, hooks, memory) while the model weights stay frozen (akshay_pachaar, _philschmid). Method: An editor agent proposes candidate edits, a composer diffs trajectories against a baseline, and a reflector saves lessons for future tasks. No grader is needed. Results: Gemini 3.5 Flash gains 8.4 points on WorkBuddy-Bench and 7.5 on JobBench. Skills and scripts make up about 50% of edits. Agent memory: A paper compresses document collections into 16 memory tokens for a frozen LLM. It beats full context on FactKG (84.33% vs 80.43%) while using 108× fewer source tokens (omarsar0). Environment synthesis for RL: Data World: Generates data-analysis environments from known mechanisms. RL on 2,135 tasks adds 20.9 points on DABstep-Hard to Qwen3.6-35B-A3B without distilled trajectories (omarsar0). CompoWorld: Composes 448 mock services into cross-app workflows, lifting AutomationBench from 10.3% to 32.3% (ZhihuFrontier). Automated discovery: Busy Beaver: A DeepMind Gemini agent found and Lean-verified acceleration rules for 11 unresolved BB(6) machines (omarsar0). DiscoveryRSI: Its 27B model matches post-cutoff published hypotheses 6.3% of the time, versus 2.5% for GPT-6 (omarsar0). Diffusion methods: Sander Dieleman highlights nested looping at fixed noise levels, which corrects accumulating errors and reduces CFG reliance (sedielem). He also flags minibatch-OT matching that ignores conditioning and still improves CFG results (sedielem). Inference Infrastructure and Systems vLLM v0.32.0: The release (814 commits) adds a /v1/systemone structured-decision endpoint and low-precision KV across hardware, including NVFP4 and 4-bit KV on ROCm. items.content: Japan launched a $578 million mission Monday on a five-year expedition to land on the largest moon of Mars and retrieve samples for return to Earth, a daring international project that could yield new insights into the formation of the Solar System. The MMX spacecraft rode into orbit atop a 207-foot-tall (63-meter) H3 rocket, Japan's flagship launch vehicle. The rocket assigned to MMX debuted a new souped-up configuration with four strap-on solid rocket boosters, full-throttle main engines, and an extended payload shroud to accommodate the demands of Japan's heaviest and most ambitious interplanetary mission to date. items.title: Fintech Funding Fell 21% In Q3 As Deals Grew Scarcer
items.author: Judy Rider
items.content: Venture funding into fintech startups slid 21.4% year over year in the third quarter of 2026, while deal count fell nearly 31%, Crunchbase data shows, pointing to a narrower funding market with fewer rounds and continued reliance on large transactions. All told, fintech startups raised $10.6 billion globally in the third quarter of 2026, down 28.4% from $14.9 billion in Q2 2026 and 21.4% from $13.5 billion in Q3 2025. The pullback comes as investors draw sharper distinctions between companies attracting capital and those struggling to raise, according to QED Investors partner Laura Bock. “The market remains bifurcated — AI vs. not and market leaders vs. not,” she said. Forerunner founder Kirsten Green similarly described capital concentrating in fewer, larger rounds, with infrastructure, payments and stablecoin rails attracting investor interest, supported by greater regulatory clarity. Deal count drops Notably, deal count in Q3 was the lowest in the quarters covered by our analysis, dating back to the first quarter of 2018. Just 687 fintech funding rounds were recorded globally in the third quarter, compared with 789 in the previous quarter and 995 in the same period a year earlier. That represents declines of 12.9% quarter over quarter and 31% year over year. Investors are demanding stronger evidence of performance before writing checks, noted Green. For Series A and B rounds, “evidence counts for more than narrative,” she said. In emerging categories, actual usage and momentum can matter more than revenue multiples. Elsewhere, investors want efficient growth, a credible path to profitability and stronger evidence of lasting customer demand before committing to a large Series B, Green said. More startups are also combining debt and equity to limit dilution. Pullback in large rounds The quarter-over-quarter funding decline was largely driven by a pullback in large rounds. Funding from rounds of at least $100 million fell 43.3%, from $9.07 billion in Q2 to $5.15 billion in Q3, accounting for approximately 93% of the overall dollar decline. Funding from rounds below $100 million declined just 5.1% sequentially. Compared with Q3 2025, funding from rounds of at least $100 million decreased 7%, while funding from smaller rounds fell 31.4%. Large transactions remained more resilient than smaller-round funding year over year. That divide also extends to pricing. Green said a small group of companies with clear momentum command aggressive valuations, while others face greater discipline. Bock pointed to Ramp and Monzo as similarly sized businesses with widely different valuations, attributing Ramp’s premium to investor enthusiasm for its AI momentum and growth trajectory. Global mega-rounds The United States remained the largest market for fintech funding last quarter. All told, U.S. startups attracted $5.38 billion, or 50.5% of the $10.64 billion global total in Q3. The next-largest markets were Singapore with $1.28 billion (12.1%); Saudi Arabia with $626.6 million (5.9%); India with $452 million (4.2%); Brazil with $352 million (3.3%); and the United Kingdom with $337.8 million (3.2%). Singapore’s total was heavily concentrated in Ant International’s $1.2 billion round. Despite the U.S. being the largest market for fintech funding, the quarter’s five largest funding rounds went to companies based outside the United States, ironically. Ant International, a Singapore-based provider of digital payments and financial services for businesses, raised the largest round in Q3 2026, a $1.2 billion Series A at a listed $11.2 billion post-money valuation. The data does not identify a lead investor but lists Alibaba Group and Ant Group as participants. Barq, a financial app provider based in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, raised a $329.5 million Series A at a $1.85 billion post-money valuation. M20 Capital, Noon Investments and Sohar International participated in the financing. Hong Kong-based Qupital, which provides financing to e-commerce businesses, secured a $300 million Series C led by M Capital at an estimated $1.36 billion post-money valuation. Jakarta, Indonesia-based Ajaib, an online investing platform, raised a $270 million Series C led by SBI Group at a $1.35 billion post-money valuation. Rounding out the top five, Riyadh-based Tabby, a digital financial services provider, raised $233 million in a Series F round led by Blue Pool Capital at a $6.5 billion post-money valuation. Late-stage fintech funding fell to $4.8 billion, down 40.4% quarter over quarter and 17.3% year over year, in Q3, per Crunchbase data. One startup lifts early-stage funding Early-stage fintech funding was comparatively resilient at $4.23 billion, up 11% quarter over quarter and down just 0.6% year over year. However, Ant International’s $1.2 billion Series A accounted for 28.4% of that total. Excluding that transaction from Q3 2026 alone, early-stage funding would have fallen 20.4% sequentially and 28.8% year over year. Early-stage deal count also dropped, from 173 in Q2 to 165 in Q3, suggesting that the increase in funding dollars did not reflect a broad expansion in activity. Fundraising expectations are rising as AI makes products faster to build and launch, Bock said. Early revenue carries less weight than sustained growth. While $1 million in annual recurring revenue once served as a common Series A benchmark, investors now want greater traction and stronger momentum, including revenue that has at least tripled over six months. “Efficiency still matters, but growth is back in focus,” she said, adding that expectations of larger potential outcomes are pushing valuations higher. Meanwhile, angel and seed funding totaled $1.12 billion, down 19.7% from Q2 and 35.2% from Q3 2025. AI reshapes investor priorities AI is primarily redirecting investment within fintech, although agents and payments are attracting some new capital, Green said. Companies without an obvious AI offering can still raise funding, but investors increasingly expect evidence that the technology improves their economics, speed or ability to reach customers. “The product has to carry that story,” she said. Bock said the distinction between companies adding AI to existing processes and those building their products around it matters. The strongest AI products deliver substantial improvements that drive rapid adoption and customers’ willingness to pay. “When investors say a company is ‘AI,’ they usually mean its growth rate is high, so growth has become the proxy,” she said. QED’s recent investments span customer support, analytics, financial advice, banking infrastructure and fraud prevention. Bock sees a durable opportunity for startups that handle the specialized integrations and accuracy requirements financial services demands — work she argues frontier AI labs are unlikely to prioritize. Green, meanwhile, said payments initiated by AI agents have moved “from ‘if’ to ‘when’” in her conversations, as major networks and processors introduced protocols to support them. She is also seeing more fintech companies seek ownership of regulated infrastructure rather than rely on outside providers. But she sees potential overfunding in stablecoin infrastructure, where many startups are pursuing the same customers, and in tools that let AI agents complete purchases for buyers, where, in her view, startup formation has outpaced transaction volume. Green sees more opportunity in the systems that make agent-driven commerce trustworthy, including fraud prevention, identity verification, agent permissions and tools that help merchants accept those purchases. “I suspect the market is treating the rails as the moat,” she said. In her view, payment infrastructure is likely to become commoditized, leaving more value with the companies that own customer relationships and earn their trust. Bock’s broader thesis is that AI could reshape financial services by sharply reducing the costs of underwriting, compliance and customer service while enabling more personalized financial products. QED is particularly interested in advice and wealth management, underwriting, insurance claims, risk and compliance, and finance back-office operations, alongside stablecoins and tokenization. “The financial services operating system will be rebuilt end-to-end,” she said. Related Crunchbase query: Global Financial Services Venture Funding In 2026 Methodology The data contained in this report comes directly from Crunchbase, and is based on reported data. Data is as of Oct. 5, 2026. Note that data lags are most pronounced at the earliest stages of venture activity, with seed funding amounts increasing significantly after the end of a quarter/year. Please note that all funding values are given in U.S. dollars unless otherwise noted. Crunchbase converts foreign currencies to U.S. dollars at the prevailing spot rate from the date funding rounds, acquisitions, IPOs and other financial events are reported. Even if those events were added to Crunchbase long after the event was announced, foreign currency transactions are converted at the historic spot price. items.title: How To Build A Billion-Dollar Company Without Venture Capital
items.author: Guest Author
items.content: By Nacho De Marco Today’s venture capital ecosystem looks markedly different from even just five years ago. Most significantly, a small number of AI companies are now attracting the vast majority of available venture capital. In Q1 2026, just four companies collectively raised $188 billion, which alone accounted for 65% of total global venture investment, per Crunchbase data. Meanwhile, in that same quarter, just 20% of global VC funding went to non-AI firms. Deal count was also down 30%, meaning that checks are being made out to fewer companies all around. So what happens to startups when the VC route is all but closed? I built a company into a multibillion-dollar business without any venture funding. Here’s a few lessons I picked up along the way: Prioritize customers and revenue, not fundraising Nacho De Marco, founding GP of BDev Ventures, and chairman of BairesDev. Many founders unknowingly treat fundraising as a measure of success. But while it’s useful, funding doesn’t result in success on its own. Achieving strong levels of customer trust is also helpful when it comes to inspiring investor confidence. High retention rates, repeat purchases and sustained engagement drive the financial fundamentals on which strong valuations are built. In B2B SaaS, for instance, companies with net revenue retention above 110% are valued at 2.4x the median. Additionally, customers provide a feedback loop that helps create the discipline every company needs, and each user is a vote of confidence that compounds over time. Going to market: Take time on pricing strategy Too many early-stage companies set prices too low because they fear that higher prices will repel customers. In my experience, however, underpricing more often signals uncertainty rather than good value. Customers want quality products and services, and they expect that the quality will be reflected in the price. Incredibly, only 22% of B2B SaaS firms conduct rigorous pricing research, and firms more commonly regret underpricing than overpricing. So at the outset, it’s important for startups to inform themselves what price their product or service can actually sustain, and then raise quality if it’s too low. Equally, in services markets where prices are more established around a norm, superior quality can be an important differentiator. At the same time, however, companies must continually resist the temptation to chase customers with ever-cheaper prices, which can start a race to the bottom. Hire the best talent Too many founders hire for speed rather than quality. Take the time needed to raise the bar with talent. Hire the right people, and they’ll help maximize every last drop of value. Many years ago, I decided to focus on just a small fraction of our applicants and hire only the top 1% of talent. When we found the best developers, it meant we could compete on delivery quality rather than just price. Keeping costs low is important, but skimping on talent is not a winning strategy. Use process automation efficiencies to drive growth One of our best decisions was to replace manual hiring processes with proprietary machine-learning systems at an early stage. Not only do these systems screen developer applications, but they can also build, match and deploy top-quality teams for each client project. This advance allowed us to cut costs associated with evaluating applications, accelerate lead times, and improve the quality of our teamwork. In parallel, we also invested in creating similar systems for our digital marketing so that growth wouldn’t require proportional increases in overhead. Whether it’s in recruitment, sales or operations, process automation can create some of the biggest drivers of growth and help bring about conditions needed for significant expansion to occur. Operate as if cash is running out tomorrow Companies thrive in challenging funding environments by operating with discipline. That means obsessing over unit economics, prioritizing activities that directly drive revenue, questioning every cost, and eliminating anything that isn’t pulling its weight. Not only does this aid growth, but it also makes a business more resilient in hard times. Financial constraints drive leaders to create efficiencies by automating workflows, streamlining processes and inventing innovative work models. Years before COVID-19 forced others to follow our lead, our company streamlined its operations and boosted scalability by developing a remote-working model. When the pandemic made remote work necessary, the fact that we already had the systems and workflows in place gave us a competitive advantage over other firms, and this in turn led to significant growth. Long term: Stay married to the problem, not the solution The past decade convinced many founders that venture capital was the default path to building a meaningful company. But while funding cycles rise and fall, the fundamental principles of good business don’t. Infusions of capital can accelerate growth, but they cannot create a great company from scratch. On the longest timescale, the most successful founders are the ones committed to solving problems rather than just selling a product and chasing funding. In a world short on funding, growth simply can’t happen without it. Nacho De Marco is the founding GP of BDev Ventures, and chairman of BairesDev, one of the largest bootstrapped nearshoring companies worldwide. Driven by his entrepreneurial spirit, he launched BDev Ventures in 2021 to help B2B companies accelerate their growth through a proprietary lead-generation platform. He also invests in and serves on the boards of biotechnology and e-learning companies. In recognition of his career path, he won distinctions such as an EY Entrepreneur Of The Year 2024 Bay Area Award. items.title: Meta Muse exposes users' personal and business secrets when they share conversations
items.author: Dan Goodin
items.content: Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through Web links, researchers reported Monday. Like many online services, Muse allows users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed. A single query is all that's required Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. items.title: Introducing tsrs: a Port of TypeScript to Rust
items.author: Boshen Chen
items.content: Cloudflare and VoidZero are now working with Max Schwenk of Owner.com on tsrs, a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler. We are doing this work in close collaboration with the TypeScript team, and incubating tsrs as part of the Oxc JavaScript compiler toolchain. Our goal is to help developers spend less time waiting for their code to be checked and more time building. Making TypeScript faster and more memory-efficient also helps bring complete development environments to more places, including right in your browser. To be clear, we are not forking TypeScript. We believe the TypeScript team should remain in full control of the language’s design and direction. They have maintained a long-term vision while guiding TypeScript’s adoption across the JavaScript community. We do not want to change that. The TypeScript team can move quite fast on many things, but for some features they may spend years intentionally exploring options and making prototypes before picking the right implementation. A Rust port has to follow those decisions closely, or it will eventually fall apart and become incompatible. We have to preserve the TypeScript language strictly based on its original implementation – and the TypeScript team should remain solely responsible for deciding what that looks like. Performance and memory improvements Early benchmarks of our Rust port of TypeScript are promising: tsrs is up to 8x faster and uses ~70% less memory compared to TypeScript 7.0 when using the same number of type check workers: As you can see, the next version of TypeScript already brings many performance improvements, making TypeScript 7.1 beta up to 2.5x faster than TypeScript 7.0. Some of these optimizations were upstreamed from tsrs, and we’re hoping to find more. You may have seen recent benchmarks of different TypeScript ports with various performance claims, often due to using larger machine types and different options compared to TypeScript’s defaults. We worked with the TypeScript team to ensure the above benchmarks are comparing the same configuration. By default, tsrs ships with an adaptive configuration dependent on the machine type that uses more memory but is even faster: Try tsrs TypeScript in Rust aims to be a faithful port of TypeScript. You can try an experimental release by installing the tsrs package from npm: npm install tsrs npx tsrs Why now? We’ve seen many attempts at porting TypeScript to other languages over the years. Because of the complexity involved, only one of the ports succeeded: the TypeScript team’s port of TypeScript from JavaScript to Go. However, frontier AI models can now do large-scale ports almost independently in a matter of days. We have now seen slopforks, faithful ports, and completely re-architected versions of TypeScript in Rust or C++. There is clearly a demand for even faster TypeScript. Why Rust? You might be thinking: “TypeScript’s Go port already made TypeScript 10x faster and far more memory efficient than the previous version written in TypeScript. Why isn’t that enough?” However, it’s not just about speed. Rust offers some unique advantages: running in WebAssembly. The Rust + Wasm story has always been strong, and one of the reasons comes down to the fundamentals of Rust’s language design. When you compile a Go program to Wasm, you have to compile Go’s garbage collector along with it. But Rust’s memory management model enables straightforward memory interactions between a WebAssembly guest and host. This is one of the key things that makes Rust a much better fit for the WebAssembly use-case: memory efficiency. Cloudflare Workers have supported Wasm for a long time. Just a few weeks ago we announced supporting native Rust in Workers with the new Emscripten target for wasm-bindgen. When you run entire software build and deployment systems in tight loops on Workers, the benefits of a small memory footprint pay off quickly. It means you can run these workloads so efficiently that it’s now possible to run fully encapsulated development systems in places where they couldn’t have been run before. This enables new possibilities when combined with agents: You are now able to run a development toolchain end-to-end in a fully sandboxed environment on Cloudflare. But with Wasm, you can also run those environments safely client-side in your browser, or on an embedded device, or an IoT application. How will the tsrs port be maintained? First, we are working with Theo Browne to merge tsc-rs and tsrs into a single package that supports all of TypeScript’s features including Language Server Protocol (LSP) and content mappers. Second, we’ve seen a lot of success with how we maintain Vinext in sync with its upstream, Next.js. We explained how we do this in a recent blog post: Each morning, an agent reviews the changes, fetches diffs, and opens tracking issues for anything that could affect Vinext. Every night, the compatibility matrix is regenerated as we run the Next.js test suite against Vinext. When one of these tests or issues reveals a gap, agents are now in the position where they can identify the change across both codebases, build a reproduction, port any relevant tests, and propose a fix. We will apply the same process to TypeScript, taking extreme care that we don’t introduce diverging behaviors from upstream TypeScript. When we come across performance improvements, we’ll attempt to contribute them back to the TypeScript Go codebase so everyone wins. Finally, we recognize that there are some differences to the upstream version of TypeScript right now, like for example the order in which diagnostics are printed. We aim to reduce those differences to a minimum by the time we publish a stable release. What’s next? Cloudflare is already the home of many free and open source Rust tools that power the JavaScript ecosystem, such as Vite, Rolldown, Oxlint, and Oxfmt. With more than 10 million developers building on Cloudflare, we care a lot about making the underlying developer toolchain faster, more portable, and easier to run in more places. We are excited to experiment with deeper tsrs integrations into our stack, for example for type-aware lint rules in Oxlint. Like with Vinext, our goal is to run tsrs as a well-maintained healthy open source project — without getting in the way of TypeScript itself. The Oxc team has already begun refactoring the codebase to make it faster, use less memory, and make it maintainable. We know the TypeScript team is taking this seriously – they are experimenting with memory and performance improvements for tsc. We are excited to collaborate with the TypeScript team and the JavaScript community to build the best and fastest implementations of TypeScript together.

items.title: How 3 Java Champions are using GitHub Copilot for increased productivity
items.author: Julien Dubois
items.content: AI coding tools can generate code quickly, but speed alone does not solve the hardest software engineering problems. Developers still need to provide context, validate results, protect maintainability, and remain accountable for what ships. To learn how experienced developers strike that balance, we spoke with three Java Champions, all with over a decade of experience in using Java. They shared concrete examples of using GitHub Copilot in production and open source, along with the practices they use to turn AI-generated output into reliable software. Here are the tips they shared with us. Meet the Java Champions Vlad Mihalcea, founder of Hypersistence and author of the book High-Performance Java Persistence Patrick Baumgartner, software crafter at 42talents with 20+ years of Java experience Frank Delporte, senior technical writer at Azul and maintainer of Foojay.io with 15+ years of Java experience Vlad Mihalcea GitHub profile: @vladmihalcea How has GitHub Copilot helped you recently? I’ve been using it to analyze, design, and implement various features in both Hypersistence Utils and Hypersistence Optimizer. For example, I’ve been wanting for a long time to develop a web application that provides Optimizer event history so we can see how performance improvement efforts are materializing in application performance. Before AI, I kept postponing this task because it would have taken me weeks to develop. But using Copilot is like having a new team member, so I used it to create an app that will ship in the next version of Hypersistence Optimizer. Instead of weeks, this task took just two days to implement. What’s your typical usage? Are you using GitHub Copilot as an IDE plugin or the GitHub Copilot app? I use GitHub Copilot in IntelliJ IDEA because it’s convenient to run while reviewing source code or during a debug session. It’s very useful as a code assistant, and it helps me speed up both investigations and building prototypes for features that need validation. I still review the plans and the code that is generated by AI since their goal is to improve my productivity, not replace me entirely. While AI provides the right answer in many situations, there are still times when the response is not satisfactory and requires my intervention. Can you share some tips and best practices? For example, which skills are you using? I created my own skills so that whatever text Copilot generates looks like something I wrote by hand. This skill captures my voice from 65 of my published articles, so a draft comes back sounding like my blog instead of like a language model. This is really useful when generating documentation for this project, since it lets the LLM learn from 12 years of blogging and provide examples that follow the same principles, such as expressiveness, testability, and simplicity. Throughout my career as a software engineer, I’ve learned that we spend far more time on code maintenance than on creating it. Therefore, because maintenance and stability are critical for existing products, I developed skills that help AI mimic existing code practices in accordance with the principle of least astonishment. One tip is to change the model type based on the type of operation. For thorough thinking, I use Opus with the 1 million context window and Extra High or Max reasoning. However, for simpler tasks, such as generating reports, release notes, or verifying documentation, I use lighter models that consume fewer tokens. Patrick Baumgartner GitHub profile: @patbaumgartner Your work involves coaching teams. What is your approach? A lot of my work happens while the normal business still has to keep running. You cannot stop everything for six months to “transform.” We usually start by solving immediate problems together, understand where the team currently stands, define where we want to go and how we will know that we are improving, and then move there step by step. Depending on the situation, that can mean Software Craft practices such as TDD, refactoring, continuous delivery and XP; architecture and modularisation with Spring Boot, Spring Modulith; Spring Security; optimising Java and Spring Boot applications for containers; or increasingly, agentic engineering. The important part for me is that I work with the team. We make decisions together. I don’t want a team to become dependent on me. Ideally, after some time they no longer need me except perhaps as a sparring partner. And maybe that explains why I find this new generation of AI tools so interesting: I like working with people, learning, experimenting, and solving problems. AI gives us another very powerful tool for doing exactly that. Can you share a good story about how GitHub Copilot has helped you recently? There are actually three very different examples that changed how I think about working with GitHub Copilot. Let’s start with the first one. One was a migration of around 900 teaching slides across 15 presentations from Reveal.js to Marp. These were not simple slides. Many contain code, animations, and even interactive examples where I can change JavaScript live while teaching. More importantly, the presentations had already been battle-tested with students. The flow worked. Losing one small piece could break the story I use in the classroom. Doing that migration manually would probably have taken me a week or more—and realistically, I might simply have avoided doing it because it was such tedious work. With Copilot, I approached it differently. We first analysed the existing material, defined the target, created a migration plan, established constraints, provided examples, and defined what had to remain intact. Then we worked from the big structural changes down into the details. The really important part was verification. We generated screenshots of the Reveal.js and Marp versions and compared them visually and algorithmically. We built a small application where I could run both slide decks next to each other to verify animations manually. We even compared the generated PDFs. That meant the agent did not just say, “Migration complete.” We had evidence. The entire migration took me roughly eight to ten hours. I still owned the content, the teaching intent, and every meaningful change. Copilot could fix a typo automatically, but if content, versions, dates or meaning changed, that was something we discussed. For me, that experience reinforced an important principle: delegate execution, not responsibility. I own the result. Can you share the second example? A second example came from building a terminal UI application with Tamboui. It initially worked perfectly in Linux under WSL, and I had completely forgotten that somebody might run it directly in Windows CMD or PowerShell. And then a real user did. They discovered that the Enter key was simply ignored in some forms. That is another principle I strongly believe in: ship software early, because you learn from how people actually use it. We used Copilot to turn that feedback into reproducible UI tests. On Linux, Copilot was navigating the application with tmux. Through working with it, I learned about psmux and could execute similar flows in PowerShell. We reproduced the problem, created a local fix, traced the real problem into Tamboui, and I submitted the upstream fix, which was merged. During this work, the test descriptions themselves became too large for the available context. So I asked Copilot to help me redesign the way the tests were represented. Instead of verbose tables containing identifiers, names and repeated descriptions, it proposed a much more compact arrow notation: step → step → input, with additional information only where it was critical. That surprised me. We were not just using AI to execute information; we were working together on how information should be represented for execution. It did not have to be maximally human-friendly. It had to preserve the semantics while being efficient for the agent. How about the third example? The third example is completely different again. Someone close to me needed to practise mathematics, and I thought: why don’t we build a small learning app? It covers addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and division with remainder for grades one through four. But I did not want to build another simple quiz application. Together with Copilot, I researched learning approaches such as spaced repetition, immediate feedback, adaptive difficulty, motivation, cooperative learning and gamification without dark patterns. Interestingly, during that research Copilot challenged one of my original assumptions. I initially wanted the application to be generic for children everywhere. The research led us toward looking at the actual school curriculum instead. I realised that the order in which topics are introduced, the operations and number ranges differ enough that making it “universal” immediately was unnecessary. So we focused on Switzerland first and aligned the progression accordingly. Because Switzerland is multilingual, the application is available in German, French, Italian and English. It also has cooperative and competitive two-player modes, and when someone gets an answer wrong, the application explains one way to solve it and brings similar questions back through spaced repetition. I deliberately chose an architecture without a backend. There is no reason for me to collect children’s personal data on a server, so the data stays on the device and the application can simply be hosted on GitHub Pages. What started as a small experiment is now being used and shared among friends. It accidentally became a little product. That experience showed me another side of Copilot: don’t only use it to implement your solution. Use it as a sparring partner to expand and challenge the solution space before you start building. How do you typically use Copilot? I actually don’t use the classic Copilot autocomplete experience anymore. My work has moved almost completely toward agentic workflows. I use VS Code when I need a tight visual feedback loop—when I want to look closely at documents, code, presentations or intermediate results and adapt the process as I go. For larger execution-oriented tasks, I often work with the coding agent from the terminal. There I am more comfortable delegating a piece of work, letting it execute, and then inspecting the complete result. The interface I choose depends mostly on the feedback loop I need. I also had a fascinating experience using the coding-agent workflow through GitHub while travelling to JavaLand. I had started exploring an idea for a Maven plugin that optimises which Spring Boot auto-configurations are loaded. During roughly a four-hour journey, I was steering the agent from my phone: giving it a task, reviewing what it had done, thinking about the next step, and sending the next instruction. By the time I arrived, I had a working Maven plugin, a CI pipeline, performance tests against a sample application, and reports that could demonstrate whether the optimisation actually worked. That was the first time I had worked that way, and I was amazed that it actually worked. I wasn’t trying to write Java on my phone. I was reviewing, deciding and steering while the agent executed. I also use MCP servers when they give me useful capabilities or context. For example, I have used Context7 for documentation, integrations with my Logseq knowledge base, and I have experimented with an MCP integration for Adobe Premiere Pro. But I don’t use MCP just because I can. If a good CLI exists, I often prefer the CLI because it feels more direct and faster to me. The agent is also not a “junior developer” in my mental model. I think of it much more as a sparring partner. But just like anyone joining a project, it first needs to be brought up to speed. Context is king. Can you share some tips and best practices? The biggest thing I would recommend is: stop one-shot prompting. For anything non-trivial, I want to understand the problem before execution starts. Quite often I explicitly ask the agent to interview me first. The purpose of that interview is to uncover assumptions and expectations that are still implicit. A good agent can execute the wrong idea incredibly quickly. That does not make the detour cheaper. I experienced this myself while working on my Spring Boot auto-configuration optimiser. Initially I wanted to support both Spring Boot 3.5 and 4.x. There were architectural differences, so we implemented both approaches. Later I realised I no longer needed the 3.5 path and removing it was painful. The lesson was simple: detours are expensive. Get the requirements right before you accelerate. Once the intent is clear, I want a plan. When I review that plan, four things matter especially to me: are assumptions visible, are verification gates defined, does the approach fit the architecture, and does it avoid unnecessary work? The second principle is to define task-specific verification gates. “Done” should not mean that the model says it is done. For a refactoring, the gates might include passing tests, proving that all intended files were handled, updating documentation and leaving no TODOs behind. For the slide migration, the gates included screenshots, visual diffs, animations, PDF output and content completeness. The gates depend on the task. The principle does not: the agent should be able to provide evidence that the work satisfies the definition of done. I recently came across a skill called unlazy that follows a similar idea: create explicit gates, work through them deliberately, and prove that they have been completed rather than taking shortcuts. The third principle is to turn your lessons into reusable skills. I have started writing and maintaining my own Agent Skills. When I learn something from an execution—perhaps the agent misunderstood a convention, a useful check was missing, or I found a better way to approach a task—I update the skill. The next time I perform that task, the lesson is already there. One example is a skill I call maintainer-audit, inspired by work in the open agent skills community. I use it across my own repositories. It checks and, where appropriate, fixes the things I expect a maintained project to have: repository documentation, CI pipelines, Dependabot configuration, CodeQL, consistent cleanup and other project standards. The goal is not to generate another audit report for me to read. It brings the repository back toward the baseline I want automatically. That makes my projects more consistent and easier to maintain. I think of these skills as living engineering knowledge rather than static prompts. The fourth principle is to put deterministic engineering tools around the probabilistic model. I have my own quality harness that wraps tools such as Checkstyle, PMD and Spring Modulith architecture checks and produces a consolidated report that the agent can consume. I can run that from hooks and let the agent iterate: change → execute checks → read findings → fix → execute again. It continues until there are no findings left. That does not mean I stop looking at the software. I still run the application, interact with it and decide whether it behaves and looks the way I expect. Sometimes I deliberately implement feature by feature because the feedback loop is much tighter. I learned that asking for everything at once because “the AI can do it” is usually a bad idea. Large, generic specifications create large, generic implementations—and cleaning them up afterwards can be harder than building smaller increments correctly. More broadly, I think we developers need to talk much more about how we use these tools. Share the experiments that worked. Share the ones that didn’t. Borrow ideas from each other and adapt them to your own context instead of looking for one universal AI development process. That is also why I like the idea of AI as a sparring partner. On a Friday night, when I want to experiment with something and no human pair is available, I suddenly have somebody—or something—I can challenge an idea with, review an approach with, or use as a very sophisticated rubber duck. But I still take those ideas back to real people. Human feedback, product understanding and real-world context remain essential. How do you think AI is changing our profession? I don’t think software engineering students should primarily aspire to become code-producing machines. They need to become strong problem solvers. They need to understand users and stakeholders, discover the real problem behind a requirement, challenge assumptions, understand products and markets, make architectural trade-offs, think critically, work in a structured way and transfer useful solutions from one context into another. The model is extraordinarily good at generating possibilities and executing things. But as a human, I usually know much more of the actual context—including the things nobody ever documented. So I want to remain in charge of shaping the solution and let the agent take over more of the execution. In that sense, I think AI is putting the engineering back into software engineering. And I like that. Frank Delporte GitHub profile: @FDelporte How did you get started in tech? I’ve been fascinated by computers since I got a Commodore 64 when I was 11. Took some side steps into video production and television work after school but turned back into coding as that video needed to be put on DVD and the very first websites… Yes, I’m that old ;-). How has GitHub Copilot helped you recently? It’s a perfect companion to evaluate pull requests and investigate bug reports. One remarkable story is about the Pi4J library that lets you build Java applications to interact with electronic components on the Raspberry Pi. In February 2026, we released V4 which has a new plugin using the Foreign Function & Memory API. We tested it thoroughly before releasing, but still, shortly after the release someone reported that using 5 input buttons doesn’t work as expected. Pushing one of the first four configured buttons triggers a code execution as expected, while nothing happens with the fifth button. This is the kind of report you don’t want to get. Nothing was visibly broken. No exception, no warning in the logs, the fifth button was simply silent. And it got worse: with the older gpiod plugin, the exact same hardware and the exact same application, worked fine. So the problem was in our new FFM code, which sits on top of the Linux kernel’s GPIO character device and talks to it through native calls. That is not the part of the codebase where you expect to find a quick answer. So I assigned the issue to the Copilot coding agent and gave it two file paths as a starting point, the provider class and FFMDigitalInput. About half an hour later there was a pull request, with an explanation I really did not expect. Each input runs an event watcher that blocks in a native poll() call, waiting for the kernel to report a change on its GPIO line. Those watchers ran in virtual threads. And a virtual thread that blocks inside a native call cannot be unmounted from its carrier thread. It stays pinned there for the whole duration of the call. A Raspberry Pi 4 has four cores, so the virtual thread scheduler has four carrier threads. Register four inputs, and all four carriers are parked in poll() forever. The fifth watcher is created, but is never scheduled. That is exactly the bug that was reported. Not “events are flaky”, but “the fifth one does nothing.” What I liked most was not the diff, it was the conversation that followed in the review. I left a comment asking Copilot to explain this in more detail: I thought the goal of virtual threads was exactly to step away from the platform thread limit? So how is this a problem that four virtual threads block the four threads on a four-core processor like the Raspberry Pi? Check the pull request for the full conversation. Copilot was able to link the use of the Raspberry Pi which has four CPU cores with the reported problem. It was able to propose a simple fix for the problem, plus some extra improvements it found during its investigation. Can you share some tips and best practices? Tell it where to look: For the Pi4J issue #622, I added two file paths. That is a tiny bit of effort that removes a huge amount of searching in a large codebase. You usually have a hunch about the neighbourhood even when you have no idea about the bug. Give it to the tool so it doesn’t need to investigate the complete code. Ask for proof and tests: “Add a unit test to validate the change” is something I ask a lot these days. Well, asked, because it has now become a rule in my instructions file. It also prevents cases where the diagnosis was wrong, because the test won’t fail on the old code. Ask why: If you don’t understand a fix, say so and ask. The explanation is a deliverable too and should be added into your project documentation or inside the ticket or pull request. It teaches everyone who reads the info later. For example, this also triggered more questions within the Pi4J team about virtual thread pinning on native calls. Stay in control: All of these pull requests in Pi4J were reviewed and approved by maintainers before they went in. That’s the model that works best in this project: the agent does the investigation, the humans stay responsible for what ships. But also for my other projects I always do a review of the code that was generated by the tool. I always want to keep code readable and maintainable. Too often, a tool creates duplicate methods or recreates something which is already available in another place and should be combined. That’s your responsibility. You can go very fast these days with AI-assisted coding, which also means you can very fast create a mess. Don’t do that, keep your code manageable, your colleagues and future-self will thank you if they have to investigate bugs or make improvements later.
